extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and standards for composing correct, clear undergraduate-level mathematical proofs, including techniques (direct, contrapositive, contradiction), case analysis, and rules of mathematical writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove conditional statements by assuming the hypothesis P and using definitions and algebra/logic to deduce the conclusion Q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof begins with the assumption that the hypothesis is true and ends with deriving the conclusion. Work forward from P using known facts, definitions, and earlier propositions. Examples in the text show typical algebraic manipulations (e.g., assume x,y positive and manipulate to get desired inequality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrapositive proof
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove 'If P then Q' prove the logically equivalent contrapositive '~Q implies ~P'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outline: 'Suppose ~Q. Therefore ~P.' Use logical equivalence P => Q ⇔ (~Q) => (~P). Start by assuming the negation of the conclusion and deduce the negation of the hypothesis. Useful when transforming information about the conclusion into information about the hypothesis is easier than the direct direction. Example provided: proving parity statements by assuming 'not odd' and deducing 'not even'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline for contrapositive proofs (explicit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Set-up and structure for contrapositive proofs: Suppose Q is not true; deduce P is not true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First line: 'Suppose Q is not true.' Last line: 'Therefore P is not true.' Between them, use logic and definitions (and possibly case analysis) to transform ~Q to ~P. Be mindful of negating compound statements via DeMorgan's laws when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove a statement P by assuming its negation ~P and deriving a contradiction (a statement C and its negation ~C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outline: 'Suppose ~P. Therefore C and ~C.' You may not know C ahead of time — do scratch work assuming ~P and derive progressively until you obtain an obvious contradiction. Any clear impossibility suffices (e.g., 1 is even and 1 is odd, or an integer expression is simultaneously an integer and not an integer). Classic examples: √2 irrational and infinitely many primes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof by contradiction for conditionals (conditional-specific outline)
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove 'If P then Q' by contradiction, assume P and ~Q and derive a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outline: 'Suppose P and ~Q. Therefore C and ~C.' This is equivalent to showing (~(P => Q)) leads to impossibility. Useful when assuming P and the negation of Q gives a direct path to contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treating multiple cases
rubrics_metrics.description: When the statement's truth depends on different possibilities (e.g., parity, sign), split into exhaustive cases and prove the claim in each case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the relevant cases (e.g., n even vs odd, a positive/zero/negative) and prove the proposition separately in each. Examples: showing 1+(-1)^{2n-1} is always a multiple of 4 by treating n even and n odd; constructing n given multiple of 4 by considering a = 0, a>0, a<0. Be explicit about which case you are handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treating similar cases and 'Without loss of generality' (WLOG)
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple cases are essentially the same except for order, it is acceptable to do one case and indicate the other(s) are analogous, typically with 'Without loss of generality...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this only when the remaining cases are nearly identical; for transparency (especially when learning), write out all cases. Avoid abbreviating the phrase as 'WLOG' in formal student writing; spell it out if used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work backwards as a proof strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: In planning a proof, it can be helpful to work backwards from the desired conclusion to an obviously true statement, then reverse the steps for the actual proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to prove 2√(xy) < x + y, square both sides and manipulate until you get (x - y)^2 ≥ 0, which is obviously true; then reverse the steps, justifying each reversal (e.g., monotonicity of sqrt with positive numbers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use previously proved results to justify algebraic operations (e.g., taking square roots)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not apply operations that change inequalities without justifying them; rely on earlier propositions when needed (e.g., taking square roots preserves '<' when both sides are positive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: after proving 4xy < (x+y)^2, use the earlier proposition that for positive numbers taking square roots preserves '<' to conclude 2√(xy) < x + y. Explicitly verify hypotheses (both sides nonnegative/positive) before applying such operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negating statements correctly (use DeMorgan's laws)
rubrics_metrics.description: When working with contrapositive or contradiction proofs, carefully negate compound statements using DeMorgan's laws and logical rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Negation of 'A and B' is 'not A or not B'. In contrapositive proofs you often need ~Q and manipulate it; in contradiction proofs with universal statements use that ~(∀x P(x)) ⇔ ∃x ~(P(x)). The text demonstrates using DeMorgan's law when negating '5∤x and 5∤y' to conclude '5|x or 5|y'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining proof techniques (proofs within proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof may use multiple methods (direct, contrapositive, contradiction) nested inside each other; adopt whichever technique is most effective for each subclaim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is common to begin with a direct proof for the main claim and use a contradiction or contrapositive for a subsidiary claim. Example: expressing a rational as a product of two irrationals used the known irrationality of √2 proved earlier by contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin each sentence with a word, not a mathematical symbol
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences should start with words (capitalized) rather than symbols, to avoid ambiguity and to respect case sensitivity of symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad examples: 'A is a subset of B.' (okay) but 'x is an integer...' starts with symbol — instead write 'The number x is an integer...' or 'Because x is an integer...'. The book gives multiple bad/good pairs showing how starting with symbols can be confusing or 'silly'.

rubrics_metrics.name: End sentences with a period (even when ending with math)
rubrics_metrics.description: Punctuate mathematical sentences like normal English sentences; end with a period even if the sentence ends in a mathematical expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical statements are phrases with special symbols — use normal punctuation. Examples illustrate placing a period after displayed or inline equations when the sentence ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate mathematical symbols and expressions with words
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid writing strings of symbols that can merge and become ambiguous; use words to separate expressions for clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare 'Because x^2 -1 = 0, x = 1 or x = -1.' (bad) vs 'Because x^2 - 1 = 0, it follows that x = 1 or x = -1.' (good). Also 'Unlike A∪B, A∩B equals ∅.' should be 'Unlike A ∪ B, the set A ∩ B equals ∅.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid misuse of symbols (do not use symbols as words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols (=, <, ∈, etc.) belong inside mathematical expressions, not as replacements for words in prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: 'Since the two sets are =, one is a subset of the other.' Good: 'Since the two sets are equal, one is a subset of the other.' Avoid constructs like 'a is € of every set'; instead 'a is a subset of every set.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using unnecessary symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not introduce symbols that clutter or obscure meaning when words suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example bad: 'No set X has negative cardinality.' Better: 'No set has negative cardinality.' Keep notation minimal and used only where it aids clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the first person plural ('we')
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer 'we' and 'us' in mathematical exposition to create a conversational, guiding tone between writer and reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is conventional in mathematics: 'We now prove...' rather than 'I' or 'you'. It invites the reader through the proof steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the active voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer active constructions to make writing livelier and more concise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: 'The value x = 3 is obtained through division of both sides by 5.' Good: 'Dividing both sides by 5, we get x = 3.' Active voice tends to be clearer and shorter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain each new symbol
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever introducing a new symbol, explicitly state its meaning and domain so the reader is not left searching the context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad: 'Since a | b, it follows that b = a c.' Good: 'Since a | b, it follows that b = a c for some integer c.' Always note 'for some integer c' or equivalent to make the origin explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch out for the pronoun 'it' (avoid ambiguity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using 'it' when the referent is ambiguous; prefer explicit nouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example bad: 'Since X ⊂ Y, and 0 < |X|, we see that it is not empty.' Which is 'it'? Better: 'Since X ⊂ Y, and 0 < |X|, we see that Y is not empty.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use conjunction words carefully ('since, because, as, for, so')
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that 'Since P, Q' asserts P is true and Q follows, which is stronger than 'If P then Q'. Ensure appropriate usage and that both statements are meaningful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These words assert the antecedent is true and are not equivalent to conditional statements. Use them only when P is indeed being asserted as true in the proof context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concluding adverbs correctly ('thus, hence, therefore, consequently')
rubrics_metrics.description: Place these adverbs before statements that logically follow from previous ones, and ensure the statement indeed follows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use them to introduce unsupported claims. Example: write 'Therefore a = 2k + 1.' not 'Therefore 2k + 1.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity is the gold standard of mathematical writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Always prioritize clarity over rigid adherence to rules; break a rule if it makes the exposition clearer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reading other proofs and adopting what works helps develop style. The book emphasizes that clarity should guide choices about notation, sentence structure, and when to be explicit vs. concise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use definition-based manipulations in algebraic proofs (e.g., congruence/divisibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving statements about divisibility or congruence, invoke the definitions directly (existence of integer multipliers) and manipulate algebraically to produce the required divisibility statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: From n|(a-b) write a-b = nc, multiply both sides by (a+b) to deduce n|(a^2 - b^2); to show ac = bc (mod n) multiply a-b = nk by c to get ac-bc = n(kc). Use the existence of integer witnesses explicitly in the prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using proof technique choice pragmatically
rubrics_metrics.description: Select the proof method (direct, contrapositive, contradiction) based on which approach simplifies transformations between hypothesis and conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show contrapositive often smoother when the conclusion implies easier algebraic manipulation (e.g., quadratics), and contradiction gives a clear starting point for universal statements. Be flexible and justify method choice by clarity and brevity.
